  • Sources indicate that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Sources indicate that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

Recent findings suggest that these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

If the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Issues with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “blueprint falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

In a recent development, what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

If pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

In a recent development, the boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

It has been revealed that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

An alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

According to recent reports, have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

Recent findings suggest that if it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

In a recent development, the biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

Sources indicate that the most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

Industry observers note that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

It has been revealed that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

It has been revealed that once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

According to recent reports, the lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

It has been revealed that now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

Sources indicate that if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

According to recent reports, if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Sources indicate that once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Industry observers note that even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid significant swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

Industry observers note that if a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Sources indicate that let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

With both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done quickly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

Technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a massive, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is vital.

Lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

It has been revealed that but, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the problem being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

According to recent reports, if you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

But what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

According to recent reports, while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a fresh stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

Industry observers note that but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

Sources indicate that I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is crucial. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

Lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

According to recent reports, if the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

It has been revealed that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

It has been revealed that speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

Industry observers note that I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

In a recent development, the climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Recent findings suggest that once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

In a recent development, see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

  • Overview: The Garmin CIRQA is an excellent screenless health band, but it suits people who dislike watches better than current Garmin watch wearers.
  • Recent findings suggest that I like wearing a major watch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Overview: The Garmin CIRQA is an excellent screenless health band, but it suits people who dislike watches better than current Garmin watch wearers. After more than two months of day-and-night testing, Outside columnist Graham Averill found it tracks sleep, heart rate and HRV, auto-detects workouts and needs charging about once a week, all for $200 with no subscription. The trade-off: you can’t see your data in real time without opening your phone.

Recent findings suggest that I like wearing a major watch. Not a fancy watch, but a big, adventure watch with large numbers and all sorts of data on the face like the altitude of my current location and how many steps I’ve taken during the day. I like wearing a big adventure watch because it sends a statement to the world. It says, “I might be standing in the grocery store checkout line with a shocking amount of ground beef in my cart, but I do cool things in the outdoors.”.

It has been revealed that also, my big adventure watch tracks all of my health data. I am a man of a certain age (50), so the world tells me constantly how crucial it is to monitor the hours I sleep and my resting heart rate. But Garmin recently released the CIRQA, a new health band that promises to track every aspect of my life, and it had me wondering if I should ditch the big, ostentatious watch and opt for a more minimalist health band. One without a face. One that sends a different statement to the world, probably along the lines of “please ask me about my meditation practices.”.

So I spent the last two months wearing Garmin’s new CIRQA health band every day, and I discovered that it is an excellent health tracker that does everything it claims to do. I also discovered that these minimalist health bands aren’t for me. But the CIRQA might be exactly what you’re looking for. Let me explain.

Pros and Cons + Comfortable design + Great battery life + Automatic workout tracking + Awesome sleep score detail + No subscription required – Can’t track data in real time.

Industry observers note that I’m all in on Garmin’s ecosystem. I wear the Garmin Fenix 7 watch, I use Garmin’s computers on my bike, and I even track my golf game with Garmin’s app and launch monitor.

According to recent reports, as I inch my way closer to death, I’ve become obsessed with knowing every aspect of my health, so I’ve been curious about comprehensive health bands like Whoop. But Whoop is expensive, with an annual subscription that starts at $199. Garmin’s CIRQA promises all of the data of a Whoop without the annual subscription.

So I spent more than two months testing the Garmin CIRQA, wearing it every day and night and charting my health on Garmin’s everything app, Connect.

The CIRQA tracks all the major data that a health-conscious athlete could want, continuously monitoring your heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV). It tracks your sleep quality, counts your respiration rate and measures your pulse ox and your skin temperature. The smart band then uses all of these metrics to deliver a “Body Battery” score that puts a number on your sleep quality, workout difficulty, and stress levels.

It’s comfortable and understated. The band is made from a soft, stretchy poly fabric that isn’t waterproof, but dries fast. I wore it on my right wrist most days—I kept my watch on my left wrist—and found it dries fast after a workout, swim or shower. It does as good a job picking up your heart rate as any wrist-based heart rate monitor I’ve tried, and the details about your sleep quality are awesome. You get a Sleep Score every morning, which contributes heavily to your Body Battery score, but you can dig deeper on Garmin’s Connect app to learn how much deep sleep or REM sleep you got, and how many times you were restless and awake throughout the night.

Industry observers note that so far, I’m restless and awake an average of 40 times a night. I think my wife is pinching me in my sleep.

Sources indicate that you can also self-report lifestyle choices to the app, like alcoholic beverages and late-night meals or snacks. This option has helped me draw a direct link between booze and poor sleep. I always suspected it—because there’s so much science to back up the theory—but I never wanted to believe it. Unfortunately, you can’t argue with math. A typical sleep score for me is in the high 70s or low 80s. Add a couple of beers toward the end of the night, and that score drops to the 40s.

Yes. I’m impressed with how well the CIRQA automatically picks up an activity. Start walking or hit the gym and the CIRQA tracks every movement, heartbeat and calorie without any prompts or button pushing. If you’ve ever forgotten to click the “start” button before an epic effort, you know that this automatic tracking is awesome. There’s nothing worse than going for a six-mile run that you didn’t track. If you don’t know your total calories burned, did it even happen?

Sources indicate that you’ll get an alert on your phone after the workout that takes you into Garmin’s Connect app, where you can name the activity. The Connect app is a massive part of CIRQA’s user interface. That’s where you can get details about each workout or nap, and it’s easy to use. Connect even has a cool coach layer, so you can design workout intends, and it tells you how much sleep you need to get to recover from your day’s effort.

It has been revealed that smart bands like the CIRQA are designed to simplify your health tracking, giving you the data you want to monitor every aspect of your life, but with one less screen to look at—the watch. But you have to open your phone to see any of that health data, which means you can’t dig into your metrics in real time.

I like wearing a watch when I work out because it tracks my heart rate and calories burned in real time. It keeps me honest and has made my workouts more effective.

My Garmin Fenix doesn’t automatically pick up my workouts, and my wife complains that her Apple Watch doesn’t do a good job of that either. The CIRQA’s battery life is great, too. I charge it once a week, about the same as my Garmin Fenix.

And that’s my takeaway from two months’ of testing the CIRQA: it’s great. The CIRQA does exactly what Garmin states it will do, but it’s not an upgrade from my watch, so I don’t see any reason to switch.

It has been revealed that but plenty of people don’t like wearing bulky watches, and many athletes don’t want or need to know their heart rate while they’re working out. If that sounds like you, the CIRQA might be a good option, especially since you won’t be on the hook for a $200 subscription every year.

#170692. Make Uphills Easier With These Exercises for Explosive Strength

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1374 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Make Uphills Easier With These Exercises for Explosive Strength

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1374 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hills don’t just feel hard.
  • It has been revealed that “On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” claims Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete.
  • In a recent development, explosive strength can be trained, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hills don’t just feel hard. Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground. If you’ve got that one hiking buddy who seems to power up the hills while you’re huffing and puffing, the reason isn’t just that they’re fit. It’s that they’ve built up power—specifically explosive strength, which is fitness jargon for their ability to rapidly muster the strength they’ve built. Explosive strength is the same stuff you use when you jump, bound, or push yourself up a steep step.

It has been revealed that “On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” claims Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete. “If you don’t have the ability to hit those little power spikes over and over and over again, that’s a much greater determinant of uphill performance.”.

In a recent development, explosive strength can be trained, though. In a small 2011 study of women in their 60s and 70s published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity, one group was assigned to lift weights in a way that would build explosive strength. After 12 weeks, those women climbed stairs 17 percent faster than they did at the beginning of the study.

“Uphills are hard, and they’re hard for everyone,” claims Mike Aidala, coach and owner of The Offense, a gym and mindset coaching business in Boulder, CO. He says that approaching your training with a goal of getting stronger, rather than faster, can help build uphill power.

Here’s a mental intent method from the study that can make every exercise build more explosive strength, and six specific exercises for building explosive, uphill strength from Viada, Aidala, and Rose Wetzel, a certified personal trainer and pro Spartan racer with multiple world championship podium finishes.

Explosive exercises are usually those where your body leaves the floor (like squat jumps or box jumps) or a weight leaves your hands (like medicine ball throws). But you can achieve the same benefit by performing the concentric phase—the “lift” phase—of any exercise with explosive intent. That’s how the elderly participants in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity study built power. On each repetition of machine exercises, they did the eccentric—or “lowering”—portion of the lift at a controlled pace, and then they pushed the weight up in an explosive manner.

Sources indicate that lifting weights in this way gives a two-way boost to your uphill performance. Not only does it build power in the “push” portion of each lift, but lowering weights slowly and under control increases the strength of your tendons.

Sources indicate that “When we train our tendons, we’re able to be more explosive,” says Wetzel. Stronger tendons, she says, “help with the body’s ability to spring off the ground, to explode off with all that strength.”.

You can use this method with almost every strength exercise you do, notes Viada. His recommendation: Start with a few sets of each exercise with explosive intent, and then move into your “regular” sets of the move. During the explosive sets, he says, don’t use as much weight as you will in the later, “normal” sets.

According to recent reports, for a starting weight, Viada suggests subtracting 25 percent from the maximum weight with which you could normally perform 10 reps. For example, if you regularly do 10 leg presses with 200 pounds, perform your explosive reps with 150 pounds.

According to recent reports, in addition to using a lower weight, Viada also recommends doing fewer repetitions in each set. While you could probably do this weight for 15 or more repetitions, start with a handful, and make sure each one is done with maximum explosive intention.

According to recent reports, “The only thing that matters is that they’re explosive and they’re fast,” he notes. “So when you go to the bottom of the movement, think about suddenly trying to push the bar or sled up through a wall. Pretend you’re trying to smash [the weight] up through the ceiling.”.

Do a few sets in this way for each move, then move to your normal, longer sets with your regular weights.

Our experts recommend these six moves to become more explosive and more stable as you trek or run uphill—they’re moves the coaches have used to train clients to climb 14ers, and that Wetzel herself has used to vault her way to multiple obstacle course race podiums.

In a recent development, the first four exercises can be done anywhere, including as part of a run or hike warmup. For the last two, you’ll need some gym equipment.

In a recent development, these jumps let you practice exploding, but also train your knee not to wobble on each step. Not only will a stable knee help prevent injuries when you’re thrown off-kilter on the trail, but will prevent you from losing energy that could be used to propel you forward.

In a recent development, do one set of 10 jumps per leg three to four times per week. Over time, try to minimize wobbling, and then increase the distance of your jumps.

Similar to the previous exercise, these jumps incorporate side-to-side movement. Don’t rush through them, Aidala indicates. Land, get stable, take a beat, then repeat.

According to recent reports, do 10 jumps in each direction on each leg. Perform these three to four times per week.

These aren’t the plodding high knees you’re used to, Wetzel says.

“When I do these drills, it’s for a very short amount of time, and I do them for power,” she says. “I’m not doing high knees like someone might do for 30 seconds to get their heart rate up … it’s like six to eight seconds of hot potato, hot potato, hot potato, and then catch my breath for 30 seconds.”.

You can do these before every run or hike, or as a warmup before any workout.

It has been revealed that this move, Wetzel says, helps you to feel like you can spring off with each step up a hill. Unlike a longer jumping lunge, she does these mini lunges as promptly as possible, keeping the movement “fierce, short, and explosive.” Instead of dropping into a full lunge, bend your knees only slightly, with your feet moving front to back almost like you’re cross-country skiing while jumping slightly.

Do a few sets of 16 reps before every run, hike, or gym workout.

“Uphill running starts from the hips,” Viada says. “And with Bulgarian split squat hops, when you start that explosiveness from the bottom, you’ll explosively engage those hips like nothing else.”.

Industry observers note that this takes one of the most dreaded moves in the gym and adds an explosive element, with the front foot leaving the ground on each repetition. Your foot doesn’t need to come way off the ground, though, Viada notes. An inch or so is great. Since it’s already a tough move, he recommends using a light weight, or no weight at all.

According to recent reports, perform three to four sets of four to five hops per leg, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these two to three times per week.

When lifting with explosive intent, coaches often recommend that you “explode out of the hole,” or the bottom of the move. With the Anderson squat, you start in the hole using a squat rack, pressing the bar off pins so you can focus even more on the powerful concentric portion of the lift.

Don’t set the stops on the rack too low, Viada indicates. Aim so that when you get under the bar, your knees are bent 90 degrees, mimicking the angles you’ll need to hike uphill with power.

Perform three to four sets of four to five squats, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these one to two times per week.

#170688. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (860 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Industry observers note that there is a cinema up north.
  • Sources indicate that this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

Industry observers note that there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

Sources indicate that this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

Industry observers note that however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

In a recent development, I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a substantial-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

Sources indicate that I watched The Alpinist on the substantial screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

It has been revealed that nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

Latest Update: A Hiker Died Trying to Help His Son After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).
  • A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.
  • The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

“On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”.

AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

It has been revealed that located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

It has been revealed that “If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard noted. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”.

Industry observers note that batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

Sources indicate that similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard stated he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

Recent findings suggest that “They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard remarked. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”.

  • Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Fresh York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.
  • It has been revealed that the day prior, Becky indicated up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Fresh York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

It has been revealed that the day prior, Becky indicated up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

New York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

But time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with plans to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

When the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

In a recent development, finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

It has been revealed that “This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”.

Foutch mentioned that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

According to recent reports, “It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch noted. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”.

According to recent reports, the hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

Industry observers note that people with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, stated there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

It has been revealed that “In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly states. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”.

Wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he states SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody quickly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”.

He indicates e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

According to recent reports, urgency is particularly notable in these cases, Cooper states. Research demonstrates that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

That’s why Cooper says, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.

Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
  • Industry observers note that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

Industry observers note that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Sources indicate that later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

It has been revealed that “At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he says. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

Recent findings suggest that “The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman indicates. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he released his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, Upcoming Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

“The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he states. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”.

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he stated, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

It has been revealed that “Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he indicates, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

Zartman notes he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design new testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.

According to recent reports, as a frequent flier who jet-sets at least once a month and camps three seasons out of the year, I’ve come to rely on “crossover” gear that bridges both worlds. And with how expensive everything has gotten, anything I buy must earn its keep on more than one kind of trip.

According to recent reports, I’ve honed a short list of my favorite gear that comes on most trips I take, from hopping on an international flight to camping with my family for the weekend. These dual-purpose items pack just as easily into a carry-on as they do into a trunk, are versatile enough for city streets and dirt trails, and make sense to use on a long layover and also around the campfire.

I bring these eight items along no matter whether I’m sleeping under the stars or in seat 23B.

Granite Gear is best known for its backpacking and paddling packs, but its most underrated product is the humble Zippditty Stuffsack. I use these zippered pouches for keeping all the little things in order while traveling and adventuring—toiletries, charging cables, snacks, pens, first aid items, tent stakes, you name it. A set of four comes with 2.4L, 1.7L, 1L, and 0.6L sizes and in a variety of fun colors. There’s rarely a trip where at least a couple of them don’t make it into my bag.

Dirty laundry stinks. Literally. That’s why I always pack a lightweight dry bag when I’m traveling and camping. Dry bags are the MVPs of kayaking and river rafting trips, keeping clothes and gear from getting wet. But they’re also my secret hack for stashing stinky clothes until I get home and can wash them. Sea to Summit makes some of my favorite durable bags, but honestly, any roll-top or drawstring stuffsack or dry bag will do the trick when it comes to sealing in the funk.

If you’re like me and refuse to pay a premium for caffeine on the go (hard pass on that mediocre-at-best $7 airport latte), let me introduce you to my go-to backpacking coffee. I tuck a few of these Alpine Start instant coffee packets into my bag on every trip. I’ve made it a habit to pack a leak-proof travel mug (my favorite is Ocean Bottle) and ask for some hot water from an airport café or flight attendant. Flavors include the classic, dirty chai, matcha, and select seasonals. Plus, they taste much better than anything on the beverage cart. Trust me. I’m a self-proclaimed coffee snob.

Hotel pillows are so hit or miss. Sometimes I get lucky with a fluffy, comfy place to rest my head. Other times I’m stuck with a flat or lumpy excuse for a pillow. You know the pain. I’ve started bringing my HEST Camp Pillow along so I can rest assured I’ll get a good night’s sleep, whether I’m in a tent, a hotel room, or 30,000 feet in the air. It comes in small, medium, and large sizes; the small is best for quick trips, the medium is worth the extra squeeze if you’re staying somewhere multiple nights in a row, and the large is my go-to for car camping. If you prefer a neck pillow on flights, the Hest Pro Travel Pillow will ruin all other neck pillows for you.

In a recent development, most bags are built for one kind of trip. The Thule Aion Duffel is built for all of them. It has been my go-to bag for more than four years on everything from car camping weekends at state parks to international flights to Japan, Copenhagen, and Mexico. Its features make sense for both time outdoors and work trips in the air: The 35L capacity easily fits a weekend’s worth of clothes and then some, and an internal divider splits the duffel into two main compartments, with a padded laptop sleeve sandwiched in between. There’s also a TPU-lined, zippered compartment that locks in odors, moisture, and dirt from hiking boots and swimsuits.

I try to stay off my phone when I’m camping, so I rarely bring a heavy-duty power bank with me. And when I travel, I don’t often need one either since I’m never far from an outlet on a seatback or airport lounge chair. Rather than lugging around a bulky battery pack, I bring the lightweight NESTOUT 5,000mAh power bank in my bag. This little stick of energy gives my electronics (phone and headphones mainly) all the juice I need on the trail and in transit. Its 5,000mAh capacity gives my phone roughly one full charge, and its 15W output tops it off swiftly if I need extra power. It’s also fully waterproof, dustproof, and shockproof.

I’ve lost count of how many times a cheap travel-sized shampoo bottle exploded in my luggage on flights and camping trips. Last year I finally invested in some reusable liquid bottles and now I no longer have to worry about a messy surprise when I unpack. Humangear’s GoToob Squeeze Bottles are made of soft, flexible silicone with a no-drip valve and a locking cap. I fill them with shampoo, conditioner, body wash, sunscreen, and even toothpaste. The wide mouth makes them easy to fill and clean, and the TSA-friendly sizes (1.7 ounces for short trips, 2.5 ounces for longer ones) always clear security.

Industry observers note that my favorite shoe for camping, traveling, and just about everything in between is the Arc’teryx Kragg. They’re super comfortable, low-key stylish, and versatile enough to wear on the trail, around town, or on the plane. Originally designed as an approach shoe for climbers with a grippy outsole, the Kragg’s slip-on upper works wonders for a midnight bathroom run at the campsite or breezing through airport security. I love that you can collapse the heel and wear them like slippers on a long-haul flight, which has saved my feet on more than one red-eye. On work trips, they even look sleek enough to wear to dinner (as long as I’m not wearing the pair that’s scuffed up from season after season of camping). Pricey? Yes. Worth the investment? 100 percent.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S.
  • Nine years later, Significant Bend is still beautiful.
  • According to recent reports, one of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: kellyvandellen/Getty Images).

The first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S. and Mexico, I was amazed not just at how beautiful it was, but how peaceful. The buff and black-streaked limestone walls soared 1,500 feet over the water, the afternoon sun streaming through the gap. The river was running low and slow, trickling over the mud and rocks, no more than knee deep. I rolled up my pant legs and waded into the water, toward that invisible line in the middle of the river that split two countries.

Nine years later, Significant Bend is still beautiful. Covering an area bigger than Rhode Island, this stretch of West Texas desert is home to some of the state’s most moving scenery, from river canyons to rocky peaks, with animal and plant life to match. Hikers willing to put in the work on the area’s rugged trails may spot javelinas rooting in the undergrowth or nocturnal, raccoon-like ringtails climbing up the cliffs and trees of the Chisos Mountains; they’ll see prickly pear cactus and ocotillo, a spindly, Seussian shrub equipped with vicious spines, growing wild in the desert flats. (That border, however, may soon be far more concrete. Read on for more on that.).

According to recent reports, one of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak. At 7,825 feet, Emory is the highest point in Substantial Bend and the Chisos, and enjoys commanding views of the terrain for miles around. Getting there, however, takes some muscle: The rough, 9.7-mile hike to the top ascends singletrack and rock stairs through oak, piñon, and juniper forest before ending with a final, dramatic scramble to the peak’s exposed summit. November, when summer’s broiling temperatures finally cool down, is an ideal time to hike it. (Note: There is no water at all along the Emory Peak Trail, and the NPS suggests hikers carry at least one liter per person per hour.).

The round trip takes about 6 to 8 hours, and you’ll want to leave some time to relax afterward. Santa Elena Canyon’s picnic area is an ideal spot for an early dinner, and cap off the night at the park’s free riverside hot springs. (Due to recent flood damage, reaching both of these highlights is right now harder than usual. The paved road between Cottonwood Campground and Santa Elena is closed at the time of writing; drivers with a true 4-wheel drive vehicle and high clearance can get there on Old Maverick Road. Due to another closure, getting to the hot springs requires a 4-mile round-trip, relatively flat hike along a gravel road. Consider it part of the adventure.).

Industry observers note that starting at the Chisos Basin Visitors Center, take the Laguna Meadows trail for about a third of a mile to a fork, where you’ll hang a left on the Pinnacles Trail. Follow it as it steadily climbs, traversing desert flats and rocky slopes with the sheer top of Emory looming in the background. After another 3.4 miles, the trail reaches a saddle below the top of the peak. Continue on the Emory Peak Trail for another 1.5 miles, then tackle a final, somewhat exposed 30-foot scramble to the top of the mountain and 360-degree views of the park below. Retrace your steps to the trailhead, or break up the hike by reserving one of the Pinnacles campsites ahead of your trip.

In an 8-1 decision on November 9, the Supreme Court approved a request by the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall through Massive Bend, ruling against plaintiffs who had argued that the barrier would decimate rare plant species and cut off migratory routes for animals, and that it risked damaging ancient rock art and Native heritage sites. In Santa Elena Canyon itself, the Department of Homeland Security plans to install vehicle barriers and surveillance infrastructure and clear patrol roads through the area. Conservation groups and state officials like Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa say they’ll continue to push to end construction in the park.

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-fresh TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

According to recent reports, the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.
